rockrose-sb: Rock Rose is made by Dunnet Bay Distillers, which Martin and Claire Murray set up in Caithness in 2014, close to Dunnet Head, the northernmost point of mainland Britain. The gin is named after Rhodiola rosea, the rose root that grows on the sea cliffs of the far north, and the couple add other botanicals found nearby, such as rowan berries and sea buckthorn, distilling it in small batches.
isleofharris-sb: The Isle of Harris Distillery opened in the village of Tarbert, in the Outer Hebrides, in 2015. It was set up by Anderson Bakewell, a man with long ties to the island, chiefly to bring steady work to a small community whose young people were leaving. Gin was its first release, flavoured with sugar kelp gathered by hand from the island's sea lochs and sold in ridged glass meant to recall the rippled sea. The distillery's single malt, The Hearach, came years later.
monkey47-sb: Monkey 47 was launched in 2010 by Alexander Stein and the distiller Christoph Keller in Germany's Black Forest. Its makers tell of Montgomery Collins, a British airman who settled in the Black Forest after the Second World War, opened a guesthouse called The Wild Monkey and made a gin of his own, and they present the brand as a revival of his recipe. The 47 counts both the botanicals, many gathered locally, including lingonberries, and the strength at which it is bottled.
ferdinandssaardry-sb: Ferdinand's Saar Dry Gin was first released in 2013 by the Avadis Distillery in Wincheringen, in the Saar and Moselle wine country of western Germany, where distiller Andreas Vallendar works with herbs grown nearby. Its signature is a finishing dose of Riesling from the Forstmeister Geltz-Zilliken estate in Saarburg, and the gin takes its name from Ferdinand Geltz, the Prussian forester remembered in that estate's name.
ginmare-sb: Gin Mare was created by the Giró family, makers of Gin MG in Catalonia, as a gin built around the flavours of the Mediterranean rather than of London. It is distilled in Vilanova i la Geltrú, a fishing town on the coast south of Barcelona, from botanicals that include Arbequina olives, Greek thyme, Italian basil, Turkish rosemary and Spanish citrus, each macerated separately before blending. Launched in the late 2000s, it rode Spain's gin and tonic boom, and Brown-Forman bought the brand in 2022.
nordes-sb: Nordés is a Galician gin, named after the cold north-easterly wind that sweeps the Atlantic coast of north-west Spain. Instead of a grain base it is built on a spirit distilled from Albariño, the white grape of the Rías Baixas, and its botanicals lean on the Galician coast and countryside, among them samphire, eucalyptus and lemon verbena. It appeared in the 2010s, as Spain's gin and tonic craze turned regional producers towards local flavours.
larios-sb: Larios takes its name from the Larios family of Málaga, one of the great industrial dynasties of nineteenth-century Andalusia, whose wine and spirits business grew up alongside their sugar and textile interests. Its dry gin became the everyday gin of Spanish bars through the twentieth century, long before the craft boom, and the brand now belongs to Suntory Global Spirits.
malfyconlimone-sb: Malfy was launched in 2016 by Biggar & Leith, a company formed the year before to develop spirits with small family-owned distilleries in Europe, and it is distilled by Torino Distillati near Turin. Its name nods to the Amalfi Coast. Con Limone, the range's lemon gin, steeps peel from Amalfi Coast and Sicilian lemons in Italian grain spirit, presses it in a traditional basket press and distils the botanicals at low temperature in a vacuum still. Pernod Ricard bought the brand in 2019.
roku-sb: Roku was launched by Suntory in 2017 as its Japanese craft gin, made at the company's spirits workshop in Osaka. Roku means six in Japanese, for the six Japanese botanicals at its heart: sakura flower and sakura leaf, sencha and gyokuro tea, sansho pepper and yuzu peel, each picked in its own season. They join eight traditional gin botanicals, and the bottle is cut with six sides as a nod to the name.
kinobi-sb: Ki No Bi comes from the Kyoto Distillery, founded by David Croll and Marc Holmes, which opened in 2016 and is described as Japan's first distillery dedicated to gin. The name means the beauty of the seasons. The gin is built on a rice spirit and cut with water from Fushimi, Kyoto's historic sake district, and its botanicals, among them yuzu, hinoki cypress, gyokuro tea from Uji, sansho and red shiso, are distilled separately in groups before being blended.
nikkacoffeygin-sb: Nikka released Coffey Gin in 2017, using the continuous Coffey stills it had brought from Scotland in the 1960s and now runs at its Miyagikyo distillery. The stills, and the gin, take their name from Aeneas Coffey, the Irish inventor who patented the design in the nineteenth century. Alongside juniper, the recipe leans on Japanese citrus, including yuzu, kabosu, amanatsu and shikuwasa, together with apple and sansho pepper, for a distinctly Japanese take on dry gin.
fourpillarsraredry-sb: Four Pillars was founded in 2013 by Stuart Gregor, Cameron Mackenzie and Matt Jones, who set up in the Yarra Valley outside Melbourne with a German copper still they named Wilma, after Mackenzie's mother. Rare Dry was the first gin they made and remains their signature, pairing juniper and coriander with Australian botanicals such as Tasmanian pepperberry and lemon myrtle, plus whole oranges in the still. The brewer Lion bought half of the business in 2019 and the rest in 2023.
archierosesignaturedry-sb: Archie Rose was founded in Sydney in 2014 by Will Edwards, who had researched distilleries in New York and at home before opening a distillery and bar in the inner-south suburb of Rosebery in March 2015. Signature Dry Gin was one of its first three spirits, alongside a vodka and a white rye, and it sets classic gin botanicals beside native Australian ones. Production moved to a larger site at Banksmeadow in 2020.
scapegraceclassic-sb: Scapegrace was founded in New Zealand in 2014 by Mark Neal, Daniel McLaughlin and Richard Bourke, and its name is an old English word for a rogue or a mischievous person. Classic is the gin the company started with, a juniper-led dry gin, and it remains the core of a range that later grew to include a black gin.
aviationamericangin-sb: Aviation was created in Portland, Oregon, in 2006 by distiller Christian Krogstad of House Spirits and bartender Ryan Magarian, who wanted a gin in which botanicals such as lavender, cardamom and sarsaparilla shared the stage with juniper. They named it after the Aviation, the pre-Prohibition cocktail of gin, maraschino, lemon and crème de violette. The actor Ryan Reynolds bought a stake in 2018 and fronted its advertising, and Diageo acquired the brand in 2020.
stgeorgeterroir-sb: St. George Spirits released Terroir in 2011 as one of a trio of gins, alongside Botanivore and Dry Rye, from the company Jörg Rupf founded in California to make fruit brandies. The aim was to bottle the smell of the forests of Northern California, using Douglas fir, California bay laurel and coastal sage alongside juniper. The distillery has worked since 2004 from a former navy aircraft hangar in Alameda, on San Francisco Bay.
junipero-sb: Junípero was first distilled in 1997 at Anchor Distilling, the small distillery Fritz Maytag had opened a few years earlier inside his Anchor brewery in San Francisco. It was among the first American craft gins of the modern era, a London dry style whose botanical recipe Anchor kept largely to itself. The name is Spanish for juniper and also recalls Junípero Serra, the Franciscan friar who founded the first Spanish missions in California.
deathsdoor-sb: Death's Door Spirits was founded by Brian Ellison in the mid-2000s around wheat grown on Washington Island, off the tip of Wisconsin's Door Peninsula, where local farmers had begun growing the crop again. The name comes from the strait between the island and the peninsula, called Porte des Morts, or Death's Door, by early French travellers for its treacherous waters and many shipwrecks. The gin keeps its recipe short: juniper gathered on the island, coriander and fennel.
empress1908-sb: Victoria Distillers on Vancouver Island launched this gin in 2017 with the Fairmont Empress, the grand hotel on Victoria's harbour; the number in its name is the year the hotel opened. Its indigo colour comes from butterfly pea flower, which turns pink when citrus or tonic lowers the pH of the drink, and its botanicals include the black tea blend served at the hotel's afternoon tea.
ungava-sb: Ungava was launched in 2010 by Domaine Pinnacle, a cider and spirits house in Quebec's Eastern Townships, and named after the Ungava Peninsula in the far north of the province. Its Nordic botanicals, among them Labrador tea, cloudberry, crowberry and wild rose hips, are gathered in the region, and the makers credit them with the gin's yellow colour. Corby Spirit and Wine bought the brand in 2018.
citadelle-sb: Citadelle was launched in 1996 by Maison Ferrand, the cognac house of Alexandre Gabriel, which won the right to use its cognac stills for gin in the months when cognac may not be distilled. It is often described as France's first craft gin. The house ties its name and recipe to an eighteenth-century genever distillery in Dunkirk, and the gin is made at the Château de Bonbonnet near Cognac, where the company also grows juniper of its own.
gvinefloraison-sb: G'Vine was created in 2006 by the oenologist Jean-Sébastien Robicquet in the Cognac region, after he had worked with Diageo on the grape-based vodka Cîroc. Instead of grain it is built on a spirit distilled from Ugni Blanc grapes, infused with the green flowers of the vine, which bloom for only a few days each June. Floraison, the French word for flowering, was the first gin of the range, and its floral, grapey style set it apart from London dry gins.
bolsgenever-sb: The Bols family opened their distillery, 't Lootsje, or the little shed, outside the walls of Amsterdam in 1575, and the company calls itself the oldest distilling brand in the world. During the Dutch Golden Age, Lucas Bols, a shareholder in the Dutch East India Company, drew on the spices it brought home for his liqueurs and genevers. The Bols Genever sold today was relaunched in 2008 from a recipe the company dates to the early nineteenth century, a malty style aimed at cocktails.
rutteoldsimon-sb: Simon Rutte set up as a distiller in Dordrecht in the nineteenth century, and since 1872 the family firm has worked from the same small building in the town centre, making genever, liqueurs and fruit spirits. Old Simon carries the founder's first name. As an oude genever it follows the older, maltier style, built on malt wine, the grain distillate at the heart of Dutch genever.
noletssilver-sb: Nolet's Silver was introduced in 2010 by the Nolet family of Schiedam, who have distilled in the town since the late seventeenth century and also make Ketel One. Carolus Nolet and his sons built it as a modern dry gin rather than a genever, with Turkish rose, white peach and raspberry giving it a fruity, floral character. Schiedam once had hundreds of distilleries, and the Nolet distillery, marked by its modern windmill, is one of the few still working there.
sloeginplymouth-sb: Plymouth Gin has been distilled on the same premises in the Barbican quarter of Plymouth since 1793, in a building known as the Black Friars distillery, and the house says its sloe gin follows a recipe from the late nineteenth century. Sloe gin itself is an English country tradition: the hard, sour fruit of the blackthorn, picked from the hedgerows in autumn, is steeped in gin with sugar until the spirit turns a deep ruby red.
gordonssloegin-sb: Alexander Gordon, a Londoner of Scottish descent, began distilling gin in 1769, and his London dry recipe went on to become one of the most familiar gins in the world. Gordon's added a sloe gin to the range in 1906, steeping sloes, the small sour fruit of the blackthorn, in gin with sugar in the manner of English country households. The wild boar on the label recalls a legend in which a member of Clan Gordon saved a Scottish king from a charging boar.
beefeaterpink-sb: Beefeater began in 1863, when the pharmacist James Burrough, who had bought a distillery in Chelsea the year before, started producing his own gin; the name, adopted later, refers to the Yeomen of the Guard, the ceremonial bodyguards of the British monarch. The distillery has stood in Kennington, south London, since the 1950s. Beefeater Pink adds strawberry to the classic London dry recipe and arrived as pink gin became a craze in Britain in the late 2010s.
gordonspink-sb: Gordon's Premium Pink was launched in 2017 by Diageo, carrying the London dry gin that Alexander Gordon first distilled in 1769 into the fruit-flavoured style then sweeping British bars and supermarkets. It adds raspberry, strawberry and redcurrant to the familiar juniper base, and its softer, sweeter profile is aimed at long drinks with tonic.
borovickakoniferum-sb: Koniferum is a Slovak borovička, the juniper spirit whose name comes from borievka, the Slovak word for juniper. Traditional borovička is made from a distillate of fermented juniper berries rather than from a neutral spirit merely flavoured with them, which gives it a sharper, more resinous character than most gins; Slovenia's brinjevec is a close cousin.
greenalls-sb: Greenall's traces its gin to 1761, when Thomas Dakin set up a distillery in Warrington, in the north-west of England, making it one of the longest-running gin names in the country. The Greenall family, brewers in the same town, took over the business in the nineteenth century, and their G&J Greenall distillery became a major producer of gin, both for its own label and for other brands. The gin business was sold in a management buyout in 2011.
whitleyneillrhubarbginger-sb: Whitley Neill was launched in 2005 by Johnny Neill, a descendant of Thomas Greenall, whose family had brewed and distilled in north-west England since the eighteenth century. The original gin carried African botanicals, baobab fruit and Cape gooseberry, and the baobab tree became the brand's emblem. Halewood bought the brand in 2009, and fruit-led versions such as Rhubarb and Ginger, pairing tart rhubarb with warming ginger, made it a familiar name in Britain's flavoured gin aisle. It is now made in the City of London.
opihrorientalspiced-sb: Opihr was created in 2013 by master distiller Joanne Moore at the G&J Greenall distillery in Warrington, as a gin built on the spices of the old trade routes rather than on citrus and flowers. Its botanicals include cubeb berries from Indonesia, black pepper from India and coriander from Morocco. The name is a variant spelling of Ophir, the distant land of riches from which, the Bible says, King Solomon's ships brought gold.
brockmans-sb: Brockmans was launched in England in the late 2000s by a small team with backgrounds in the drinks industry, who wanted a gin that tasted different from the London dry mainstream. Its signature is fruit: blueberries and blackberries sit alongside juniper, coriander and citrus peel, giving it a darker, berry-led profile than most gins, and it is sold in a tall, dark bottle.
silentpool-sb: Silent Pool Distillers began making gin in 2014 in restored farm buildings on the Albury Estate in Surrey, beside the spring-fed lake that gives the gin its name and its water. Founded by Ian McCulloch and James Shelbourne, the distillery heats its copper still with a restored wood-fired steam boiler. The pool itself carries a legend, retold in a Victorian novel, of a woodcutter's daughter who drowned there fleeing King John. The gin's botanicals include local honey, lavender and chamomile.
drumshanbogunpowder-sb: Drumshanbo Gunpowder Irish Gin comes from The Shed Distillery, which PJ Rigney opened in 2014 in a former jam factory in Drumshanbo, County Leitrim, billed as the first distillery in Connacht for more than a century. The gin followed in 2016, built around slow-dried gunpowder green tea, named for its tightly rolled leaves that resemble pellets of shot. Botanicals inspired by the founder's travels in the East, such as Chinese grapefruit and kaffir lime, sit alongside Irish meadowsweet.
dinglegin-sb: Dingle Gin comes from the Dingle Distillery, founded in 2012 on the Dingle Peninsula in County Kerry by Oliver Hughes, a co-founder of Dublin's Porterhouse brewing group, as one of the first new independent distilleries of Ireland's spirits revival. The gin is flavoured with local botanicals such as rowan berry, fuchsia, bog myrtle, hawthorn and heather from the Kerry hills. Hughes died in 2016, and the distillery remains with the Porterhouse group.
amazzoni-sb: Amazzoni was created in the 2010s by a group of founders in Rio de Janeiro, with the Argentine bartender Tato Giovannoni helping to develop the recipe, and it is made on a former coffee farm in the Paraíba Valley of Rio de Janeiro state, in what has been described as Brazil's first distillery devoted to gin. Its botanicals pair juniper with Brazilian ingredients such as cocoa, Brazil nut, maxixe and Victoria amazonica seed.
inverrocheclassic-sb: Inverroche was founded by Lorna Scott at Still Bay, a small town on South Africa's southern Cape coast, where she began distilling gin with botanicals from the fynbos, the dense native shrubland of the Cape Floral Kingdom. Its gins put fynbos at the centre of their identity during the South African craft gin boom of the 2010s, and Classic is the house's flagship, its juniper set beside Cape botanicals.
musgrave11-sb: Musgrave is a South African gin, distilled in Cape Town by a company that builds its spirits around African ingredients and flavours.
jaisalmer-sb: Jaisalmer was launched in the late 2010s by Radico Khaitan, the Indian spirits company that grew out of the Rampur distillery in Uttar Pradesh, founded in the 1940s. It is named after the desert city of Jaisalmer in Rajasthan and was aimed at drinkers at home and abroad who were looking for an Indian craft gin. Its botanicals mix classic juniper and coriander with Indian ingredients such as Darjeeling green tea, vetiver and lemongrass.
greaterthan-sb: Greater Than was launched in 2017 by Nao Spirits, the Goa company founded by Anand Virmani and Vaibhav Singh, and is widely described as India's first craft gin. It arrived when gin in India mostly meant mass-market bottles, and a wave of small Indian producers followed. Greater Than is the company's London dry style gin, setting Indian botanicals such as ginger and lemongrass beside the classics, and the company later added a premium gin called Hapusa.
strangersons-sb: Stranger and Sons comes from the Third Eye Distillery in Goa, founded by Rahul Mehra, Sakshi Saigal and Vidur Gupta, and was released in 2018 as part of the first wave of Indian craft gins. Its botanicals are sourced from around the subcontinent, with citrus such as gondhoraj lime from Bengal and Indian spices including black pepper and nutmeg giving it a distinctly local character.
songcai-sb: Sông Cái, Vietnamese for mother river, is a gin from a Vietnamese-owned distillery that builds its spirits on native ingredients and works with growers and Red Dao herbal practitioners in the northern uplands of Lào Cai.
paperlantern-sb: Paper Lantern is catalogued as a Singapore gin, from a city whose young gin scene draws on the herbs and spices of its Malay, Chinese, Indian and Peranakan kitchens.
brasslion-sb: Brass Lion Distillery opened in Singapore in 2018, founded by Jamie Koh, and was billed as the city's first standalone gin distillery. Its Singapore Dry Gin set out to bottle the flavours of the island's mixed food culture, with botanicals such as torch ginger flower, laksa leaf, pomelo and lemongrass alongside juniper. The lion in its name recalls Singapura, the old name, meaning lion city, from which Singapore takes its own.
chasegbextradry-sb: Chase Distillery was founded in 2008 by William Chase, the Herefordshire farmer who had earlier created Tyrrells crisps, after a trip to the United States convinced him his potatoes could become vodka. GB Extra Dry followed in 2012, a juniper-forward gin built on the farm's own potato vodka. Diageo acquired the business in 2020, and in 2025 production moved from Herefordshire to the Cameronbridge distillery in Fife, Scotland.
absolut-sb: Absolut's name goes back to Lars Olsson Smith, the nineteenth-century Stockholm spirits entrepreneur who introduced Absolut rent brännvin, or absolutely pure brännvin, made by repeated rectification, in 1879, the year from which the brand dates itself. The state monopoly Vin & Sprit revived the name a century later for an export vodka, launched in the United States in 1979 in a clear bottle modelled on an old apothecary flask, with the lettering printed straight on the glass.
absolutelyx-sb: Absolut Elyx was introduced in the early 2010s as a single-estate version of Absolut, made only from winter wheat grown on the Råbelöf estate in southern Sweden, near the company's distillery at Åhus. Its spirit is distilled in a manually operated copper column still dating from the 1920s, and copper runs through the brand, from its pineapple-shaped cups to its bar programmes. It is the luxury expression of the vodka that Vin & Sprit launched for export in 1979.
absolutcitron-sb: Absolut Citron was launched in 1988, two years after Absolut Peppar became the brand's first flavoured vodka, and it was one of the first lemon vodkas to reach a wide market. It is closely tied to the modern Cosmopolitan: the bartender Toby Cecchini has said he built his version at the Odeon in New York that year using the new Citron, though others claim earlier forms of the drink. Like the original Absolut, it is made in Åhus in southern Sweden.
smirnoffno21-sb: Smirnoff began in Moscow in 1864, when Pyotr Smirnov founded a vodka distillery that pioneered charcoal filtration and was reportedly a favourite of the Russian court. After the revolution his son Vladimir fled and rebuilt the business abroad under the French-style spelling Smirnoff, and in the 1930s the American rights passed to Rudolph Kunett and then to Heublein, which made it a global brand. No. 21 is the flagship vodka, and Smirnoff is no longer made in Russia.
stolichnaya-sb: Stolichnaya, whose name means of the capital, traces its origin to the Soviet Union in 1938, though its earliest confirmed production dates from 1948, and it became one of the Soviet Union's best-known exports. After the Soviet collapse its ownership was disputed between the Russian state and the private SPI Group, so two versions now exist: one made in Russia for the home market, and one sold abroad and made in Latvia. In 2022, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, SPI renamed its version Stoli.
beluganoble-sb: Beluga Noble was created in 2002 at the Mariinsk distillery in the Kemerovo region of western Siberia, a plant dating from the turn of the twentieth century, and it was conceived from the start as a luxury Russian vodka. It takes its name from the beluga sturgeon, the great fish prized for its caviar, and a metal beluga is fixed to every bottle. The makers say the spirit rests for several weeks after blending before it is bottled.
russianstandard-sb: Russian Standard was founded in 1998 by the entrepreneur Roustam Tariko, who set out to build a premium vodka brand for post-Soviet Russia; exports followed two years later. The name points to the nineteenth-century standards for Russian vodka that the brand links to the chemist Dmitri Mendeleev, a connection historians treat with caution. In 2006 the company opened a large distillery in Saint Petersburg, where the vodka is made from winter wheat.
greygoose-sb: Grey Goose was dreamed up in 1997 by Sidney Frank, an American importer who saw room for a vodka priced above the market leaders and chose France for its culinary prestige. He worked with François Thibault, a cognac cellar master, who developed the recipe in the Cognac region using soft winter wheat from Picardy and spring water from Gensac-la-Pallue. A frosted bottle with geese in flight completed the pitch, and Frank sold the brand to Bacardi in 2004.
ciroc-sb: Cîroc has been made in France since 2003, developed by the oenologist Jean-Sébastien Robicquet with Diageo as a vodka distilled from grapes rather than grain. Its base comes from Mauzac Blanc and Ugni Blanc grapes, and the spirit is distilled five times, the last in a copper pot still. The name blends the French words cime, summit, and roche, rock. From 2007 a long marketing partnership with Sean Combs made it a familiar nightlife name in the United States.
belvedere-sb: Belvedere was first produced in 1993 at the Polmos Żyrardów distillery west of Warsaw, a plant built in 1910, and was launched in the United States in 1996, marketed as the first super-premium vodka. It is made from Polish Dankowskie rye and named after the Belweder Palace in Warsaw, the image of which appears on the bottle. The luxury group LVMH bought into the brand in 2002 and later took full control.
chopinpotato-sb: Chopin was created in the 1990s at a distillery in Siedlce, in the farm country of eastern Poland, as a vodka that would show off a single raw material, and it is named after the composer Frédéric Chopin. Potato was its first spirit and remains the house signature, made from potatoes grown in the surrounding region and distilled four times. The Dorda family, who run the distillery, later added rye and wheat versions to show how the base ingredient changes a vodka's taste.
chopinrye-sb: Chopin Rye comes from the same family-run distillery in Siedlce, eastern Poland, that created Chopin potato vodka in the 1990s and named it after the composer Frédéric Chopin. The rye version was added later to show how much the base ingredient can change a vodka, and it is made from Dankowskie rye, a variety long grown on the Polish plains, where rye has been the traditional vodka grain for centuries.
wyborowa-sb: Wyborowa's makers trace their distilling in Poznań to 1823, and the brand took its name from a Polish adjective meaning choice or fine, first used of the vodka in an admiring press notice and then adopted for the label. In 1927 it became one of the first vodkas registered as an international trademark, and in the decades after the Second World War it was Poland's leading export vodka, especially in Britain. It is made from rye and now belongs to Pernod Ricard.
zubrowkabisongrass-sb: Żubrówka takes its name from żubr, the Polish word for the European bison, because the herb that flavours it, bison grass, grows in the Białowieża Forest on the border with Belarus, where the animals graze. Flavouring vodka with the grass is an older country practice, but commercial production of bison grass vodka began in 1928. Today the Polmos Białystok distillery makes it, with a hand-picked, naturally dried blade of the grass in every bottle.
sobieski-sb: Sobieski is named after Jan III Sobieski, the seventeenth-century king of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth remembered for leading the relief of Vienna from an Ottoman siege. The vodka is a pure rye spirit made from Dankowskie rye and produced at the large distillery in Starogard Gdański, in Pomerania, whose history reaches back to the nineteenth century. Its makers built it into an export brand, and the actor Bruce Willis later became its international face.
luksusowa-sb: Luksusowa, meaning luxurious, has been made continuously since 1928, which makes it one of the oldest Polish vodka brands still in production. It is a potato vodka, distilled from Polish potatoes, the raw material that had become a staple of the country's distillers. When Poland's borders shifted westward after the Second World War, production moved to its present home in Zielona Góra, in the west of the country.
starka10-sb: Starka, from the Polish word for old, is an aged rye spirit known in Poland and Lithuania since at least the fifteenth century, and later a favourite of the nobility of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Tradition held that when a child was born, the family sealed home-made spirit in an oak barrel that had held Hungarian wine and buried it, to be opened at the child's wedding. Modern Starka is aged in oak with small additions of apple and linden leaves, and Starka 10 has rested for ten years.
nemiroff-sb: Nemiroff takes its name from Nemyriv, a town in Ukraine's Vinnytsia region, where vodka making is first recorded in 1752. A distillery opened there in 1872 under Count Grigory Stroganov and was later run by his daughter, Princess Maria Shcherbatova, until the Soviet state nationalised it in 1920. The Nemiroff name returned after Ukrainian independence, and the brand grew into one of the country's largest exporters of horilka, the Ukrainian word for vodka.
khortytsa-sb: The first bottles of Khortytsa left a new distillery in Zaporizhzhia in December 2003, a year after the entrepreneur Yevhen Chernyak began building it. The vodka is named after Khortytsia, the island in the Dnipro river beside the city, once the stronghold of the Zaporozhian Cossacks and now regarded as a national landmark. Exports began in 2006, and in the United States it is sold as Khor.
finlandia-sb: Finlandia was established in 1970 by Alko, Finland's state alcohol company, as a vodka for the export market. Its barley spirit is distilled at Koskenkorva, in the farm country of western Finland, and blended at Rajamäki, near Helsinki, with water from the glacial spring beside the distillery Dr Wilhelm Juslin founded there in the late nineteenth century. The original bottle, designed by Tapio Wirkkala and textured to suggest ice, made Finnish design part of the brand.
koskenkorva-sb: Koskenkorva Viina reached Finnish shops in 1953, made at the state distillery that had opened in the village of Koskenkorva, in Ilmajoki, western Finland, in 1938. Finns call it viina rather than vodka, and know it simply as Kossu. It is made from local barley by a long continuous distillation, then cut with spring water and a very small amount of sugar; the export version without sugar is sold as vodka, and the same spirit is the base of Finlandia.
reyka-sb: Reyka began in 2005, when the Scottish distillers William Grant & Sons set up a small distillery in Borgarnes, in western Iceland, to make a premium vodka with an Icelandic identity. The spirit is distilled in a Carter-head still, filtered through lava rock and cut with spring water from a lava field, and the distillery runs on Iceland's geothermal energy. Its name shares an Icelandic root, meaning smoke, with Reykjavík.
ketelone-sb: Ketel One vodka was introduced in 1983 by Carolus Nolet, of the family that has run a distillery in Schiedam, near Rotterdam, since the late seventeenth century. He named it after Distilleerketel number 1, the original coal-fired copper pot still at the distillery. Made from wheat and partly distilled in copper pot stills, it was developed with the American market in mind, and Diageo bought a half share in the brand in 2008.
titoshandmade-sb: Bert Beveridge, known as Tito, began making flavoured vodkas as gifts before starting commercial production in 1997 at the Mockingbird Distillery in Austin, under his company Fifth Generation, often described as the first legal distillery in Texas. He distilled his vodka from corn in small pot stills, and the brand's breakthrough came in 2001, when it won a double gold medal at the San Francisco World Spirits Competition. It is still made at the expanded distillery in south-east Austin.
skyy-sb: Skyy was launched in San Francisco in 1992 by Maurice Kanbar, an inventor and entrepreneur who set out to make an exceptionally clean, neutral vodka through his choice of distillation and filtration. Its cobalt blue bottle made it instantly recognisable on back bars through the 1990s. Production was first contracted out in California, and after the Campari Group acquired Skyy Spirits in 2009 the business was renamed Campari America.
crystalhead-sb: Crystal Head was conceived in 2008 by the actor Dan Aykroyd and the artist John Alexander, who shared a fascination with the legend of the thirteen crystal skulls. Alexander designed the skull-shaped glass bottle, and Aykroyd set out to make a vodka without additives, which is produced in Newfoundland and filtered through quartz crystals known as Herkimer diamonds. Some retailers initially refused to stock the bottle.
purity34-sb: Purity is a Swedish vodka made at Ellinge Castle in Skåne, in the far south of the country, from wheat and malted barley, and the 34 in its name refers, the producer says, to the 34 levels of copper its heart spirit passes through during distillation.
snowqueen-sb: Snow Queen is a wheat vodka from Kazakhstan, whose northern steppe is one of the great grain belts of Central Asia.
zyr-sb: Zyr is a Russian grain vodka, distilled and filtered in the clean, neutral style that dominates the category.
haku-sb: Haku was introduced by Suntory in the late 2010s as a Japanese craft vodka made entirely from Japanese white rice. Haku means white in Japanese, a reference to the polished rice at its base. The rice spirit is filtered through bamboo charcoal, a material long used in Japan for purifying water, and the vodka belongs, with Roku gin, to Suntory's range of Japanese craft spirits.
robertocavalli-sb: Roberto Cavalli vodka is an Italian grain vodka that carries the name of the Florentine fashion designer.
42below-sb: 42 Below was founded in 1999 by Geoff Ross, a Wellington advertising executive who, the story goes, began distilling vodka in his garage. The name refers to the line of latitude 42 degrees south, which runs through New Zealand, and the brand sold itself on the country's clean water and air and on cheeky, irreverent advertising. It is made from wheat, and Bacardi bought the company in 2006.
brokenshed-sb: Broken Shed is a New Zealand vodka distilled from whey, the liquid left over when milk is turned into cheese, which puts a by-product of the country's large dairy industry to use. The brand is based in Wanaka, and takes its name from the rustic old shed on the shores of Lake Wanaka where its makers say the idea began.
fairquinoa-sb: FAIR was founded in 2009 by Alexandre Koiransky to make spirits from Fairtrade-certified ingredients, and its quinoa vodka was billed as the world's first Fairtrade-certified vodka. The quinoa comes from cooperatives of small farmers on the Bolivian Altiplano, high in the Andes, and is shipped to France, where the spirit is distilled in the Cognac region. The company has since added gin, rum and liqueurs made on the same fair-trade principle.
bacardicartablanca-sb: Bacardí began in Santiago de Cuba on 4 February 1862, when Facundo Bacardí Massó, a merchant from Sitges in Catalonia, and his brother José bought a small distillery. Facundo set out to make a lighter, smoother rum by filtering and ageing it, and fruit bats roosting in the rafters gave his wife Amalia the idea for the bat emblem. Carta Blanca, the house's white rum, became a classic base for the Daiquirí and the Mojito; after the revolution the family carried on outside Cuba, chiefly from Puerto Rico.
bacardicartaoro-sb: Carta Oro is the gold rum of the house Facundo Bacardí Massó founded in Santiago de Cuba in 1862, aged in oak to an amber colour and a rounder vanilla and caramel character. The company prospered in Cuba for nearly a century and became one of the island's largest businesses, until the revolutionary government confiscated its Cuban assets. By then Bacardí already had distilleries abroad, and the rum is now made chiefly in Puerto Rico.
bacardi8-sb: Bacardí 8, also called Reserva Ocho, is a blend of rums aged for at least eight years. According to the company, it was long kept for the Bacardí family and their guests before being offered for sale. It descends from the rum business Facundo Bacardí Massó founded in Santiago de Cuba in 1862, whose bat emblem still sits on the label, and it now ages in the Caribbean heat at the company's Puerto Rico home.
havanaclub3anos-sb: Havana Club was created in 1934 by the Arechabala family, whose distillery at Cárdenas, on Cuba's north coast, dated from the nineteenth century. The company was nationalised without compensation in 1960, and since 1993 the Cuban state and Pernod Ricard have sold Havana Club worldwide through a joint venture. A rival Havana Club, made in Puerto Rico by Bacardí from the Arechabala recipe, is sold in the United States, and the trademark has been disputed for decades. Años 3 is a young rum made for Cuban cocktails.
havanaclub7anos-sb: Havana Club 7 Años is the aged flagship of the rum brand the Arechabala family created in Cárdenas, Cuba, in 1934. After the revolution the brand passed to the Cuban state, which exported it mainly to the Soviet bloc, and in 1993 it entered a joint venture with Pernod Ricard that took it to world markets. The rum is aged in Cuba and blended by the island's maestros roneros, the master rum makers who train their successors through long apprenticeships.
havanaclubselecciondemaestros-sb: Selección de Maestros is a Havana Club blend chosen by the Cuban maestros roneros, the master rum makers who oversee the island's rums and hand their knowledge down through long apprenticeships. Each master selects aged rums for the blend, which is then given a final period of ageing in oak before bottling. It belongs to the brand the Arechabala family created in Cárdenas in 1934, now made by the Cuban state in partnership with Pernod Ricard.
santiagodecuba11-sb: Ron Santiago de Cuba takes its name from the eastern Cuban city where Facundo Bacardí founded his rum business in the nineteenth century, often called the cradle of Cuba's light rum style. After the revolution the city's distilling was nationalised, and the Santiago rums are now made by the state corporation Cuba Ron. The 11 is the age statement of this blend, aged for at least eleven years in oak.
appletonestatesignature-sb: Rum has been recorded at Appleton Estate, in the Nassau Valley of central Jamaica, since 1749, and the estate counts itself the oldest continuously operating distillery on the island. J. Wray & Nephew bought the estate in 1916 and built its blended rums into a national brand, and since 1997 they have been overseen by Joy Spence, widely described as the first woman to become master blender in the spirits industry. Signature, the house's entry blend, marries pot and column still rums from the estate.
appletonestate12-sb: Appleton Estate 12 Year Old comes from the Nassau Valley estate in St Elizabeth, Jamaica, where rum production is first recorded in 1749. The land was settled as a sugar plantation after the English conquest of Jamaica, and it has belonged to J. Wray & Nephew since 1916. Master blender Joy Spence builds the blend from rums aged at least twelve years in the valley's tropical heat, where casks lose far more to evaporation than in cooler climates.
appletonestate21-sb: Appleton Estate 21 Year Old is among the oldest regular releases from the Jamaican estate where rum is first recorded in 1749, and every rum in it has aged at least twenty-one years in oak in the Nassau Valley. J. Wray & Nephew, founded in Kingston in 1825, took over the estate in 1916 and built up its aged stocks. Joy Spence, who joined as chief chemist in 1981 and became master blender in 1997, assembles it from pot and column still rums.
wraynephewoverproof-sb: J. Wray & Nephew began in 1825, when John Wray opened the Shakespeare Tavern in Kingston and started blending and selling rum. In 1860 he took his nephew, Charles James Ward, into partnership and renamed the business J. Wray & Nephew; Ward went on to win medals for its aged rums in London and to add sugar estates to the firm. Its unaged white overproof became a fixture of Jamaican life, used in cooking and family rituals as well as in drinks.
smithcross-sb: Smith & Cross carries the name of a London firm of sugar refiners and rum merchants that the brand traces back to 1788, when the city's docks handled much of the Caribbean rum trade. The modern rum was revived in 2009 by the American importer Haus Alpenz as a traditional Jamaican rum, blended from heavy pot still styles made at Hampden Estate in Trelawny. Its intense, funky character quickly won it a following among cocktail bartenders.
hampdenestate8-sb: Hampden Estate was founded in 1743 by Archibald Stirling in the Queen of Spain valley of Trelawny, Jamaica, and became famous for slow-fermented, high-ester rums, methods credited to George McFarquhar Lawson in the nineteenth century. For most of its history it sold its rum in bulk to blenders and brokers. It began bottling under its own name only after the Hussey family bought it in 2009 and started ageing stock on site, with Luca Gargano's Velier distributing the releases. The 8 Year Old is aged in Jamaica.
worthypark109-sb: Worthy Park Estate, in Lluidas Vale in the parish of St Catherine, central Jamaica, was established in 1670 and is one of the oldest sugar estates on the island. The Clarke family has owned it since 1918; after years without a distillery, they built a new one in 2005 and began making rum on the estate again. The 109 in this bottling's name is its strength on the American proof scale, and it is a single-estate pot still rum.
coruba-sb: Coruba grew from a Swiss connection. In 1929 a Basel rum house, founded by the merchants Jules Fiechter and Peter Bataglia in 1889, set up The Rum Company in Kingston, Jamaica, to make rum for European markets under the Coruba name. The brand is now part of J. Wray & Nephew, the Jamaican rum house behind Appleton Estate.
myerssoriginaldark-sb: Myers's Original Dark was created in 1879 by Frederick Louis Myers, who founded his rum business in Jamaica and gave it his name. Its rich, dark blend became closely associated with Planter's Punch. Eustace Myers, the founder's grandson, sold the business to Seagram in 1954; Diageo later owned it, and the Sazerac Company bought it in 2018.
mountgayeclipse-sb: Mount Gay's oldest surviving deed dates from 1703, and the company calls itself the oldest commercial rum distillery in the world. The name honours Sir John Gay Alleyne, who managed the Barbados estate for his friend John Sober and was commemorated in its name after his death in 1801. Eclipse, the house's signature blend, was developed in the early twentieth century and named for the solar eclipse and the passing of Halley's comet in 1910. Rémy Cointreau has been the majority owner since 1989.
mountgayxo-sb: Mount Gay XO, once labelled Extra Old, draws on rums aged for roughly eight to fifteen years at the Barbados distillery whose oldest surviving deed dates from 1703. John Sober bought the Mount Gilboa estate in 1747, and it was later renamed in honour of Sir John Gay Alleyne, the friend who ran it for him; the Mount Gay name has stayed on the island's rum for more than two centuries. The XO blends pot and column still rums in the classic Barbadian way.
doorlys12-sb: Doorly's began as a rum label of Martin Doorly and Co., a Barbados merchant house, and is one of several old island brands that passed to R.L. Seale and Co., the firm Reginald Leon Seale founded as a rum merchant and blender between the world wars. Today Doorly's is made at Foursquare, the distillery the Seale family later opened in the parish of St Philip, and the 12 Year Old blends pot and column still rums aged in ex-bourbon barrels and then in oloroso sherry casks.
foursquaredoorlysxo-sb: Doorly's XO is part of the heritage range kept alive by the Seale family at Foursquare, the distillery David Seale established in the parish of St Philip, Barbados, on the site of an old sugar factory. The Doorly's name came to the family through R.L. Seale and Co., whose rum blending business had gathered several old Barbadian labels over the decades. The XO is a blend of pot and column still rums aged in ex-bourbon barrels and finished in oloroso sherry casks.
therealmccoy5-sb: The Real McCoy rum honours Bill McCoy, the Prohibition-era sea captain who ran liquor from the Bahamas to Rum Row off the American coast and took pride in never watering it down. The phrase the real McCoy is older than he is, but his reputation for honest, unadulterated goods attached it to him in popular memory. The brand was launched in the 2010s by the documentary filmmaker Bailey Pryor, with rums distilled and aged at Foursquare in Barbados; the 5 is aged for five years.
plantationxaymaca-sb: Plantation rums were launched in 1999 by Maison Ferrand, the cognac house of Alexandre Gabriel, which in 2017 bought the West Indies Rum Distillery in Barbados and a third of the company behind Jamaica's Clarendon and Long Pond distilleries. Xaymaca, the Taíno name for Jamaica, is a blend of pot still rums from those two Jamaican distilleries. After criticism of the word plantation and its links to slavery, the range was later renamed Planteray.
eldorado12-sb: El Dorado is the premium label of Demerara Distillers, formed in 1983 by the merger of Guyana Distilleries and Diamond Liquors and based in Georgetown. The name recalls the legend of a city of gold that explorers, Walter Raleigh among them, once sought in the Guiana interior. The 12 Year Old blends rums from several of the company's historic stills, which preserve the house styles of plantations that once lined the Demerara coast.
eldorado15-sb: El Dorado 15 Year Old was among the earliest releases of the range that Demerara Distillers, formed in 1983, created to show off Guyana's aged rums. Its blend draws on the company's rare wooden stills, among them the Port Mourant double wooden pot still and the Enmore wooden Coffey still, survivors of old sugar estates whose marks are still produced at the Diamond distillery. Demerara rum's dark, rich style was long a mainstay of the Royal Navy's rum ration.
eldorado21-sb: El Dorado 21 Year Old is one of the oldest regular releases from Demerara Distillers, the Guyanese company formed in 1983 from a merger of the country's leading distillers. Diamond, where the rum is made, was established as a sugar plantation and distillery in 1753 and runs Coffey stills alongside wooden stills moved there from estates that have since closed. Every rum in the blend has aged at least twenty-one years in the tropical heat of the Demerara coast.
lemonhart151-sb: Lemon Hart, a merchant born in Penzance in Cornwall, is credited with supplying rum to the Royal Navy from 1804, and the firm he built in London became one of the great names of the navy rum trade. The brand's 151 is a Demerara rum from Guyana, long a staple of tiki bartenders, who used it as a float and in recipes such as the Zombie. The Lemon Hart name has changed hands several times, but its rum has stayed rooted in the dark Demerara style.
angostura1919-sb: The 1919 in this rum's name comes from a house story: casks distilled that year are said to have survived a fire at the Fernandes family's distillery in Trinidad in 1932, and the rum blended from them was named after their vintage. The Fernandes business later became part of the House of Angostura, the bitters makers who had moved from Venezuela to Port of Spain in the late nineteenth century. Today's Angostura 1919 is a mellow blend of aged column still rums.
angostura7-sb: The House of Angostura settled in Port of Spain in 1875, half a century after Dr Johann Siegert first compounded his aromatic bitters in the Venezuelan town of Angostura, now Ciudad Bolívar. Best known for those bitters, the company also became Trinidad's main rum producer, especially after it bought Fernandes Distillers in 1973. Angostura 7 Year Old is a blend of column still rums aged for at least seven years in ex-bourbon barrels.
ronzacapa23-sb: Ron Zacapa was created in 1976 to celebrate the hundredth anniversary of the founding of Zacapa, a town in eastern Guatemala, and its blends were developed by the chemist Alejandro Burgaleta for Industrias Licoreras de Guatemala. The rum is made from concentrated virgin sugarcane honey and aged in a solera system high in the mountains near Quetzaltenango, under master blender Lorena Vásquez. The 23 on the label refers to the solera, which combines rums of different ages, the oldest up to 23 years.
ronzacapaxo-sb: Zacapa XO is the premium expression of the Guatemalan rum created in 1976 to mark the centenary of the town of Zacapa. Like Zacapa 23 it is aged in a solera system in the highlands near Quetzaltenango, at what the company calls the House Above the Clouds, before a final rest in French oak casks that once held cognac. The blends are overseen by master blender Lorena Vásquez, and Diageo markets the brand internationally.
botranreserva-sb: Botran comes from five Botrán brothers, who emigrated from Burgos in Spain and founded the Industria Licorera Quezalteca in Quetzaltenango, Guatemala, in 1939. Their company later merged with other family firms to form Industrias Licoreras de Guatemala, which also makes Zacapa. Botran Reserva is aged in a dynamic solera, inspired by the way sherry is aged in Spain, in which young rum is added to older rum across a series of casks.
flordecana12-sb: Flor de Caña, Spanish for sugarcane flower, grew from Nicaragua Sugar Estates, founded in 1890 at Chichigalpa at the foot of the San Cristóbal volcano, which appears on the label. The Italian-born entrepreneur Francisco Alfredo Pellas was its majority shareholder, and rum was first made there in small quantities for employees and partners; the Flor de Caña brand itself was created in 1937. The Pellas family still owns the company, and the 12 Year Old is aged in ex-bourbon barrels.
flordecana18-sb: Flor de Caña 18 Year Old is one of the oldest releases of the Nicaraguan rum made at Chichigalpa, beneath the San Cristóbal volcano, since the founding of Nicaragua Sugar Estates in 1890. The company came through the Sandinista years, when the Pellas family's businesses were taken over by the state; Carlos Pellas Chamorro chose to stay in the country, and by the end of that period the distillery was said to hold one of the largest reserves of aged rum in the world. The properties were returned to the family in 1992.
ronbarceloimperial-sb: Barceló was founded in Santo Domingo in 1930 by Julián Barceló, who had arrived from Mallorca the year before with his brother Andrés. A hurricane destroyed the distillery the following year; Andrés left for Puerto Rico, but Julián rebuilt and grew the business, which he handed to his nephew Miguel in 1974. Imperial, released in 1980, became the company's flagship, a blend of rums aged for up to ten years.
brugal1888-sb: Casa Brugal dates its founding to 1888, the year in this rum's name, when Andrés Brugal Montaner, a Catalan who had learned rum-making in Santiago de Cuba, set up in business before settling in Puerto Plata on the Dominican Republic's north coast. The company was long run by his descendants, and the Scottish spirits group Edrington took control of it in 2008. Brugal 1888 is double aged, first in American oak and then in Spanish oak casks that held sherry.
matusalemgranreserva15-sb: Matusalem was founded in Santiago de Cuba in 1872 by the brothers Benjamín and Eduardo Camp, who brought from Spain the solera method of blending used for sherry and brandy. The name is Spanish for Methuselah, the biblical patriarch famed for his long life. After the Cuban revolution the family took the brand into exile, and Matusalem is now produced in the Dominican Republic. Gran Reserva 15 is built on that solera tradition.
donqcristal-sb: Destilería Serrallés traces its rum to 1865, when Juan Serrallés imported a still from France to Hacienda Mercedita, the family's sugar plantation near Ponce in southern Puerto Rico. The family launched Don Q, named after Don Quixote, Cervantes's errant knight, in 1932, and it became one of the island's best-known rums. Don Q Cristal is the house's white rum, aged and then filtered clear.
donqanejo-sb: Don Q takes its name from Don Quixote, and it was launched in 1932 by the Serrallés family of Ponce, who had been making rum at Hacienda Mercedita since the previous century. It became one of the best-selling rums on the island, and Destilería Serrallés is still family-run. Don Q Añejo is a blend of rums aged in American oak, a step up from the house's white and gold rums.
rondelbarrilito3star-sb: Ron del Barrilito has been made by the Fernández family at Hacienda Santa Ana in Bayamón since 1880, which makes it the oldest Puerto Rican rum brand still in production. Pedro Fernández, who had studied in France, began making rum for family and guests, and the story goes that visitors kept asking for the rum from the little barrel, ron del barrilito, which became the name. Three Stars is the original blend, aged in oloroso sherry casks; the stars follow a French brandy custom he learned there.
paloviejo-sb: Palo Viejo is a long-standing Puerto Rican white rum that began with Barceló Marqués y Compañía, a company based in Arecibo on the island's north coast, before it was sold to Destilería Serrallés of Ponce, the makers of Don Q. Little has been published about its early history. It became one of the island's everyday rums, and a familiar name in Puerto Rican television advertising and sports sponsorship.
rhumclementvsop-sb: Homère Clément, a doctor and politician from Martinique, bought the Habitation Acajou estate at Le François in 1887, and the family later turned it to making rhum agricole, distilled from fresh sugarcane juice rather than molasses. The estate, now Habitation Clément, became one of the island's leading rum houses, and its gardens and old cellars are open to visitors. Clément VSOP is aged for at least four years in oak, under the Martinique AOC rules granted to the island's agricole rums in 1996.
rhumjmvo-sb: Rhum JM comes from Habitation Bellevue at Macouba, on the far northern tip of Martinique, where cane grows on the volcanic slopes below Mont Pelée. The estate takes its initials from Jean-Marie Martin, who bought it in 1845, and it is now one of the island's most remote agricole distilleries, making rhum from fresh cane juice. JM VO is aged for at least three years in oak, as the island's AOC rules require for the grade.
neissonblanc-sb: The Neisson distillery was founded in 1931 by the brothers Jean and Adrien Neisson at Le Carbet, on the Caribbean coast of Martinique, and it has stayed in the family ever since, a rarity among the island's rum houses. It makes rhum agricole from cane grown on its own land, fermented and distilled in a small column still, and in recent decades it has also become known for organic rhum. The Blanc is its unaged white rhum.
rhumdamoiseau-sb: Damoiseau's distillery stands on the former Bellevue plantation at Le Moule, on Grande-Terre in Guadeloupe, an estate established late in the nineteenth century by a planter named Rimbaud from Martinique. The Damoiseau family bought it in 1942 and founded the distillery that carries their name, and they still run it. It is the last distillery on Grande-Terre, and makes rhum agricole from fresh sugarcane juice.
rhumbarbancourt5star-sb: Dupré Barbancourt, from the cognac country of the Charente in France, founded his distillery in Haiti in 1862 and applied the cognac method of double distillation to fresh sugarcane juice. After his death the business passed to his wife, Nathalie Gardère, and her nephew Paul, and the Gardère family has run it ever since, through the 2010 earthquake that destroyed many of its ageing barrels. The Five Star, labelled Réserve Spéciale, is aged for around eight years in oak.
clairinsajous-sb: Clairin is Haiti's rustic cane spirit, made at hundreds of small village distilleries from native cane varieties, wild fermentation and traditional stills. Clairin Sajous comes from Michel Sajous's Chelo distillery at Saint-Michel-de-l'Attalaye, in the north of the country, where he grows his own cane. It reached the wider world in 2014, when the Italian bottler Luca Gargano of Velier released it in a series called The Spirit of Haiti, introducing clairin to bartenders far beyond the island.
clairincommunal-sb: Clairin Communal is a blend of clairins from several small Haitian distilleries, released by Luca Gargano's Velier as a companion to the single-distillery bottlings that first carried clairin abroad in the 2010s. Each component is made in the traditional village way, from native cane varieties fermented with wild yeasts and distilled without filtration. As the name suggests, the blend presents clairin, long drunk almost entirely within Haiti, as a shared national tradition rather than the work of a single still.
chairmansreserve-sb: Saint Lucia Distillers was formed in 1972 when the Barnard family's distillery at Dennery merged with the Roseau distillery, and it is now the island's only rum producer, working in the Roseau Valley on the west coast. The Barnard family remained at the heart of the business, and Chairman's Reserve became its flagship, a blend of rums from both pot and column stills, aged in oak.
admiralrodney-sb: Admiral Rodney comes from Saint Lucia Distillers, formed in 1972 from the merger of the island's last two distilleries, and is named after Admiral George Brydges Rodney. Rodney sailed from Gros Islet Bay in Saint Lucia to defeat a French fleet at the Battle of the Saintes, in the closing years of the American Revolutionary War. The company presents it as a premium sipping rum, blended from aged pot and column still stocks at its distillery in the Roseau Valley.
goslingsblackseal-sb: James Gosling sailed from England in 1806 with goods bound for America, but when his ship's charter ran out he put in at Bermuda and set up shop there instead. The family began blending rum in 1860 and soon developed a dark, full-bodied Old Rum, sold first from the barrel and then in Champagne bottles salvaged from the British garrison's officers' messes and sealed with black wax. Customers asked for the black seal rum, and the name stuck. Goslings holds the trademark for the Dark 'n Stormy.
riversroyalegrenadian-sb: Rivers rum is made at the River Antoine Estate in St Patrick, in the north-east of Grenada, a sugar estate dating from the late eighteenth century that is often cited as the oldest functioning water-powered distillery in the Caribbean. A water wheel still crushes the cane, the juice ferments in open tanks, and the spirit is distilled in wood-fired pot stills. Rivers Royale is the estate's bottling of this raw cane spirit, sold mostly on the island.
cruzansinglebarrel-sb: Cruzan traces its rum to 1760 and Estate Diamond on St Croix, then part of the Danish West Indies, and the Nelthropp family has managed the distillery for eight generations through many changes of ownership. The name echoes Crucian, the word for a native of St Croix. Single Barrel is the brand's premium blend: rums aged from five to twelve years are married and then rested again in new oak, one barrel at a time.
pussersgunpowderproof-sb: Pusser's was founded in 1979 by Charles Tobias, who won the Admiralty's blessing to recreate the rum the Royal Navy had issued to its sailors until the last daily tot in 1970, and set up blending and bottling on Tortola in the British Virgin Islands. Pusser is naval slang for purser, the officer who issued the ration, and a share of sales goes to a Royal Navy sailors' fund. Gunpowder Proof recalls the old test in which rum poured on gunpowder that still lit was proof it had not been watered.
captainmorganspiced-sb: The Seagram company created Captain Morgan rum in 1944 and named it after Sir Henry Morgan, the seventeenth-century Welsh privateer who raided Spanish ports and later served as lieutenant governor of Jamaica. Original Spiced arrived in the United States in 1984 and made the brand a household name; Diageo bought it in 2001, and its rum is now made in the US Virgin Islands. In Jamaica, J. Wray & Nephew holds the rights and makes Captain Morgan locally.
krakenblackspiced-sb: Kraken was introduced in 2010 by Proximo Spirits of New Jersey, with a base rum from Trinidad blended with a mix of eleven spices that includes cinnamon, ginger and clove. It is named after the kraken, the giant sea monster of Scandinavian legend, and its bottle borrows the shape of a Victorian rum flask with two loop handles, while the label shows a giant squid under its scientific name, Architeuthis dux. Its inky colour and sea-monster branding set it apart on the shelf.
sailorjerry-sb: In 1999 the tattoo artists Ed Hardy and Mike Malone, protégés of Norman Collins, the Honolulu tattooist known as Sailor Jerry, teamed up with Steven Grasse of the Philadelphia agency Quaker City Mercantile to form Sailor Jerry Ltd. The company launched a spiced navy-style rum with Collins's hula girl artwork on the label, honouring a man whose bold designs helped shape the American traditional style before his death in the 1970s. William Grant & Sons bought the rum business in 2008.
malibu-sb: Malibu was created in 1978 by Tom Jago of International Distillers and Vintners, at first in Curaçao, as a coconut-flavoured rum drink meant to make piña coladas easier to mix. When it took off, production moved to Barbados, where the rum comes from the West Indies Rum Distillery, the column still distillery George Stade built on the beach at Blackrock in 1893. Pernod Ricard has owned the brand since 2005. Despite its Caribbean image, it is named after the California beach town.
stroh80-sb: Stroh was founded in 1832 by Sebastian Stroh in Carinthia, then part of the Austrian Empire, and later moved to Klagenfurt. With no tropical colonies to supply real rum, Austria-Hungary regulated its own Inländer-Rum, or domestic rum, made from local spirit flavoured and coloured to suggest the Caribbean original, and Stroh became its most famous name. Stroh 80 is used mainly as an ingredient, in baking and in hot drinks such as Jagatee, and the name has become a byword for the style in German-speaking countries.
ronmielguanche-sb: Ron miel, or honey rum, is a speciality of the Canary Islands, where sugarcane was grown long before the Caribbean rum trade took shape. It is a sweet blend of rum and honey that must contain at least two percent honey, and the Canary Islands government protects the style under the name Ronmiel de Canarias. Guanche takes its name from the Guanches, the islands' indigenous people before the Spanish conquest.
ypiocaouro-sb: Ypióca was founded in 1846 by Dario Telles de Menezes, a Portuguese immigrant, at Maranguape in the north-eastern state of Ceará, and it grew into what is described as the oldest continuously active private company in Brazil. The family business expanded into farming and mineral water while keeping cachaça at its heart, and Diageo bought the Ypióca brand in 2012. Ouro, meaning gold, is aged in wooden casks, which give it the colour of its name.
leblon-sb: Leblon was launched in 2005 by the entrepreneur Steve Luttmann and named after the beachside neighbourhood of Rio de Janeiro, as part of a push to bring premium cachaça to cocktail bars outside Brazil. It is distilled from fresh sugarcane juice in Minas Gerais, the inland state with the country's deepest tradition of artisanal cachaça, and briefly rested in French oak before bottling. Bacardi later took over the brand as the caipirinha spread through cocktail menus abroad.
sagatiba-sb: Sagatiba was launched in the early 2000s by the Brazilian entrepreneur Marcos de Moraes as one of the first cachaças designed for an international premium market rather than the domestic everyday trade. Its sleek bottle and branding set out to change cachaça's image abroad at a time when the caipirinha was spreading through cocktail bars in Europe and North America. The Campari Group bought the brand in 2011.
novofogosilver-sb: Novo Fogo, Portuguese for new fire, is an organic cachaça from Morretes, a small town in the state of Paraná in southern Brazil, where the Serra do Mar mountains meet the Atlantic rainforest. It reached the United States around the turn of the 2010s, part of a wave of premium cachaças that followed the caipirinha abroad. Silver is the unaged expression, distilled in copper alembics and rested without wood to keep the fresh character of the cane.
avuaamburana-sb: Avuá was founded in 2013 by Pete Nevenglosky and Nate Whitehouse, who partnered with master distiller Katia Espírito Santo at her family's small distillery in Carmo, in the hills of Rio de Janeiro state. The cachaça is made in copper alembics from sugarcane grown on the property. Amburana takes its name from one of the native Brazilian woods that cachaça makers have long used for ageing, which gives warm notes of cinnamon and clove.
pitu-sb: Pitú has been made since 1938 in Vitória de Santo Antão, in the north-eastern state of Pernambuco, and takes its name from the pitu, a freshwater prawn of the region's rivers, which appears on the label. Produced in large column stills, it became one of the most familiar industrial cachaças in Brazil and it built a strong export market, particularly in Germany, where it remains a well-known name.
ronabuelo12-sb: Ron Abuelo comes from Varela Hermanos, the company founded by José Varela Blanco, a Spanish immigrant who started the first sugar mill of newly independent Panama, at Pesé in Herrera province, in 1908. His sons began distilling rum in the 1930s, and the family still runs the Hacienda San Isidro, where the cane is grown and the rum is made. Abuelo is Spanish for grandfather, and the 12 Year Old is aged in American oak barrels.
guarocacique-sb: Guaro is Central America's name for a clear cane spirit, and in Costa Rica its production has been in state hands since the mid-nineteenth century, when the government took it over to curb illegal distilling and set up the Fábrica Nacional de Licores. Since 1980 the factory has sold it as Guaro Cacique, cacique being a Taíno word for a chief, and it is the classic base of the guaro sour.
groguedesantoantao-sb: Grogue de Santo Antão is a bottling of Cape Verde's traditional cane spirit from the island most closely tied to it. On Santo Antão, cane grows in steep valleys such as Paul and is crushed in a trapiche, a cane press once turned by oxen, before it is fermented and distilled in small stills. The name grogue is usually traced to the English word grog, and the spirit is also the base of ponche, sweetened with sugarcane molasses.
bataviaarrackvanoosten-sb: Batavia arrack is the cane spirit of Java, named after Batavia, the Dutch colonial name for Jakarta, where it was made from sugarcane molasses fermented with red rice. Shipped home by the Dutch East India Company, it became a favourite base for the punches of seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Europe and later for Swedish punsch. Van Oosten is a modern bottling of the style, brought to American bartenders by the importer Haus Alpenz as interest in historic punch recipes revived.
